title: NIST IR 8596 (Initial Preliminary Draft): Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (Cyber AI Profile)

policy_extraction.issuing_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
covered_actors: Organizations using standalone or integrated AI technologies (builders and acquirers across all sectors)
Cybersecurity programs, CISOs, cybersecurity practitioners, and AI developers
Third-party AI suppliers, external service providers, and value-chain partners
Organizational leadership and human-in-the-loop (HITL) security analysts

evidence.quote: Integrate AI-specific risks into the organization's formal risk appetite and tolerance statements. Update risk appetite and tolerance on a regular basis as the nature of AI systems evolve.
Establish and communicate specific strategic risk response options (e.g. mitigations, avoidance) tailored for unique AI-related risks, such as prompt injection, model inversion, and data poisoning.
Continuously evaluate AI cybersecurity defense capabilities to ensure they are sufficiently mature to use for their intended purpose before deployment.8
practices by implementing prompt tests, adversarial tests, and evaluation gates; block deployment if safety or quality drops during performance monitoring.
Feed adversarial ML research and AI red-team reports into detection pipelines to enhance detection capabilities and support response and recovery efforts.
Before adopting a third-party AI solution, conduct AI-specific due diligence and adversarial testing to assess model vulnerabilities, ethical alignment, and performance impact.

Notification processes are established for AI-related incidents (e.g., adversarial attacks, unexpected model failures) to rapidly inform internal teams and external suppliers of incidents, such as compromised models or data.
Establish protocols for sharing AI-specific threat intelligence and incident metrics (e.g., adversarial inputs)

Communicating the intended use and known limitations of AI is critical to effective usage. Understanding how it makes decisions, when it makes mistakes, and what to do when it makes mistakes are communicated to users.
Require vendors to disclose both model and data scope, as well as incident support for AI tools.
General Considerations: Use of AI Software Bill of Materials (AI SBOM) to enhance transparency and accountability in AI components.

Organizations should use version control processes to record any change to the hardware, software, configuration values, or training data. Review and log changes to the model, training data, and the model configuration settings (e.g., hyperparameters) for cybersecurity defenses that use AI.

Minimize the use of sensitive data in AI prompts and features and implement the use of runtime redaction and guardrails. Prevent data leakage by implementing output filtering, pattern detection, and access control.
AI systems may need their own identities and credentials (i.e., AI service level accounts) to interact with a broader system. Organizations need traceability between AI systems and their actions.
General Considerations: A human is assigned responsibility for the actions of an AI system.
Gate AI-initiated network changes and privilege use by implementing human approval or policy-based checks.

General Considerations: LLMs or AI Agents may have access to data sources or tools that a user typically would not have. Bind agent and service identities to their credentials using cryptographic signing and mutual authentication.
Apply the principle of least privilege to AI agents by granting only the permissions necessary to carry out their role.
The integrity of training and input data (part of the data supply chain) should be verified to detect and prevent data poisoning and tempering.
Maintain provenance of AI datasets. Modified data could indicate data poisoning has occurred. Training data originates outside the organization can introduce additional uncertainties.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 212 provides voluntary guidance to help organizations manage, reduce, and communicate 213 cybersecurity risks.
While the Cyber AI Profile provides insights to help organizations make decisions, it is up to 929 each organization to determine its priorities and how to achieve the outcomes in the CSF Core.

policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Initial Preliminary Draft of NIST IR 8596 (Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence / Cyber AI Profile), published December 16, 2025 for public comment through January 30, 2026 (quarantined as draft_consultation until final publication). Maps all 106 NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategories across GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, and RECOVER into three Focus Areas: Securing AI System Components (Secure), Conducting AI-Enabled Cyber Defense (Defend), and Thwarting AI-Enabled Cyber Attacks (Thwart), with Priority 1–3 ratings and detailed controls for agentic AI identity, least-privilege scoping, code-execution sandboxing, and autonomy kill-switches. Complements the NIST AI RMF and forthcoming SP 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS).

risk_framing.rationale_summary: NIST IR 8596 (Cyber AI Profile) is dominantly framed around consumer_public_safety, centering on operational system resilience and protecting organizations, infrastructure (such as power grids and OT/ICS), and users from AI-related failures, data leakage, poisoning, prompt injection, deepfake phishing, and AI-accelerated cyberattacks. Consumer_public_safety narrowly edges out innovation_enablement, which is a strong runner-up emphasizing adaptable, voluntary, technology-neutral guidance that enables organizations to strategically adopt AI and capitalize on AI-enabled cyber defense efficiencies. National_security serves as a clear third frame through explicit attention to advanced persistent threats (APTs), offensive cyber operations, autonomous attack agents, AI-orchestrated espionage, and critical infrastructure resilience, with minor supporting roles for economic welfare, privacy/civil liberties compliance, and machine-speed autonomous cyber risks.
